Talking to audioXpress editor João Martins, Andreas Ehret retraces a career that led from audio coding to immersive sound. After studying electrical engineering in Karlsruhe, he joined Fraunhofer IIS in the MP3 and AAC years, then co-founded Coding Technologies in 2000 around Spectral Band Replication, the technique that made aacPlus and, in 2003, the MPEG-4 HE-AAC profile. Dolby bought the company in 2007, in what Ehret considers perhaps its most successful acquisition, and he became vice president of engineering, bringing Dolby Digital Plus, AC-4 and Atmos to consumer devices.

Atmos, developed from around 2009 and first heard in cinemas in 2012, came from rethinking cinema sound: rather than piling on channels (9.1, 22.2), engineers mixed sound objects into space. Ehret insists Atmos is not an effect or an algorithm but an end-to-end chain from mixing room to playback device, branded as an experience. Music followed, starting with a Kraftwerk Blu-ray; close work with labels and studios helped win Apple over.

Ehret then gave up his VP title to become the first employee of Dolby’s automotive unit, working with suppliers such as DSP Concepts, Cinemo and Harman. After the studio, he says, the car may be the best place to hear music. Dolby deliberately designs no loudspeakers and offers no upmixer, but it shapes speaker layouts, down to slim headrest speakers reaching 150 Hz. In China, in-car video is the bigger story. By the time of the interview, some 20 car brands had signed on.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from “Interview: Andreas Ehret – The Road to Dolby Atmos” by João Martins, published in audioXpress (2024). Read the original.
